Attendees: Ethan Miller (Redwood AE), Priya Anand (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Redwood Solutions), Liam Chen (Solstice CTO), Aisha Patel (Solstice Head of ML), Marco Ruiz (Solstice SRE), Nora Blake (Product), Samir Doshi (Infra)
summary: Technical deep dive on p95/p99 tail latency for Solstice Tech's chat/assist workload. Discussed streaming vs non-streaming paths, KV cache hit strategies, batching windows, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem network hops. Agreed next steps: run Redwood-hosted benchmark against Solstice preprod, share security docs, and follow up with a Dedicated pilot proposal.
topics: p95 vs p99 expectations and SLOs
quantization: 8-bit vs 4-bit impact on latency and quality
VPC/on-prem network hops and egress costs
transcript:
[00:00] Ethan Miller: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a deep dive on the p95/p99 behavior you saw in your dashboard.
[00:12] Liam Chen: Yeah thanks, we've been seeing bad tails—p99 spikes like 700ms when our target is sub-200 for assistant use.
[00:25] Priya Anand: Can you remind us of the call profile? streaming or non-streaming? avg tokens?
[00:33] Aisha Patel: It's mixed, main product uses streaming for UX, fallback non-streaming for batch jobs. avg seq is about 120 tokens, 95th is ~350.
[00:45] Carlos Vega: Perfect, that matters for kv cache hit rates and batching. If prefix lengths vary a lot, cold KV cache hits will show in tails.
[00:58] Marco Ruiz: Our infra's EKS on AWS, we push to a NLB fronting pods, outbound goes through a NAT gateway to Redwood hosted endpoints in us-west-2. Could that be the network hop adding to p99?
[01:12] Priya Anand: Network hops definitely add jitter. NAT + cross-AZ egress can add 10-60ms variability; but p99 at 700 suggests something else layered—maybe batching windows or cache misses.
[01:28] Nora Blake: We noticed tails correlate with lower QPS periods which seemed counterintuitive.
[01:35] Ethan Miller: That's classic: during low QPS, smaller batches cause serialization overhead per request. Also autoscaler cold-starts if you scale to zero. Do you scale pods down aggressively?
[01:46] Samir Doshi: We scale down to 1 replica at night, but not zero. Still see spikes during low traffic.
[01:54] Priya Anand: 1 replica is okay but if the runtime has heavy model warm-up (kv init, quant kernels), the first requests can pay that cost. Also streaming path can add per-chunk overhead—are you using small chunk sizes?
[02:06] Aisha Patel: Yes, chunk size is 32 tokens for streaming. We thought that would help UX.
[02:13] Carlos Vega: Small chunks increase per-token overhead in some runtimes. For p99-sensitive UX, consider slightly larger chunks or hybrid: start with a small chunk then increase.
[02:25] Liam Chen: Can you explain kv cache behavior? we thought caching would make tails better but it seems inconsistent.
[02:33] Priya Anand: KV cache helps a lot for autoregressive decoding when prefixes repeat. But miss penalty depends on placement: if KV is on-GPU and warmed, it's fast; if you're reloading from CPU or remote, that can add 100s of ms.
[02:48] Marco Ruiz: We're using a sidecar to persist KV to SSD between requests. There's a reload time when a pod gets a new model or is recreated.
[02:56] Priya Anand: Right, SSD-backed reloads can be ~150-300ms depending on model size and kernel. That's visible at p99. Redwood's runtime supports persistent KV in GPU memory for Dedicated deployments which reduces that.
[03:12] Ethan Miller: Two angles: reduce cold reloads (keep pods warm, prefetch KV), and optimize batching to avoid tiny batches. We'll send a suggested config for your traffic mix.
[03:24] Nora Blake: What about quantization? Could moving to 4-bit help the latency? We're worried about quality regressions.
[03:32] Carlos Vega: 4-bit can dramatically reduce kernel latency and memory pressure, often improving p95/p99 but at potential quality drop. We typically recommend evaluating 8-bit first; many workloads achieve 95-98% parity with int8.
[03:46] Aisha Patel: We need to measure generation quality on our evals. If 4-bit knocks down p99 from 700ms to 250ms but reduces accuracy too much, it's not worth it.
[03:56] Priya Anand: Agreed. We'll include quantization benchmark runs in the lab test and show ROUGE/EM/perplexity relative to your eval set.
[04:06] Liam Chen: Streaming vs non-streaming—do you route them differently in Redwood?
[04:12] Priya Anand: There's different code paths. Streaming keeps a persistent connection and can yield earlier tokens while non-streaming waits for full generation. Streaming has more frequent network writes which can add jitter, but improves perceived latency. Non-streaming can be optimized with batching and async pipelines for better server-side throughput.
[04:28] Marco Ruiz: Could the NLB and our VPC endpoints be causing packetization or delayed ack issues? We saw occasional retransmits.
[04:36] Priya Anand: Possibly. Packet loss and retransmits amplify p99. We usually recommend using VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for minimal public egress and to reduce NAT-induced variability. Also enable TCP keepalives and tune MTU if you're doing gRPC streaming.
[04:50] Ethan Miller: For Dedicated/on-prem, you remove those public egress hops entirely which usually tightens tails. But you trade off engineering and infra cost.
[04:59] Nora Blake: We talked about Dedicated earlier—what's the break-even for us?
[05:04] Carlos Vega: It depends on QPS and desired SLO. If you need consistent sub-200ms p99 and have steady traffic, Dedicated with GPU local KV and tuned kernels is often worth it. We'll model cost vs hosted in the follow-up.
[05:16] Aisha Patel: Can we talk about batching windows? we're currently at 20ms wait, max batch 16.
[05:23] Priya Anand: 20ms is aggressive; at low QPS it yields small batches. Consider adaptive batching: increase wait to 40-60ms under low load and drop it when QPS rises. Redwood runtime supports adaptive policies that optimize for p99 while capping added latency.
[05:39] Marco Ruiz: Any tips for monitoring to detect root-cause of spikes? We're mostly seeing tail numbers in Grafana but need finer signals.
[05:47] Ethan Miller: Instrument per-hop latencies: client->LB, LB->pod, pod decode, kv load, network egress. Collect kernel-level timings from the runtime and correlate with deployment events. We can share an observability dashboard template.
[06:00] Liam Chen: Can you run a benchmark against our preprod? we can provide creds and traffic generator.
[06:07] Ethan Miller: Yes we'll run a 1-hour bench capturing p50/p95/p99, streaming and non-streaming, with and without kv warm, and quantization variants. We'll need histogram of sequence lengths and typical concurrency.
[06:19] Samir Doshi: We'll share seq hist and a traffic replay.
[06:22] Priya Anand: Great. We'll also try both chunk sizes for streaming to show tradeoffs.
[06:29] Nora Blake: About security—what docs do you need for Dedicated or Private?
[06:34] Carlos Vega: SOC2, ISO, KMS integration notes, VPC peering and PrivateLink diagrams. We'll attach our compliance pack.
[06:42] Aisha Patel: Also RBAC and audit log retention—our security team will ask.
[06:47] Ethan Miller: We'll include those.
[06:50] [07:00] (short technical screen-share; logs/diagrams referenced: "solstice-bench.xlsx", "redwood-dedicated-arch.pdf")
[07:12] Priya Anand: One nit: if you use sidecar-based kv persistence, ensure the IO path is async and doesn't block request threads. We've seen blocking persistence spike p99.
[07:24] Marco Ruiz: Oof, yeah our current sidecar blocks on write on shutdowns.
[07:29] Priya Anand: That will show as tail events during deploys. Try graceful draining with pre-warm strategy or persistent GPU resident KV.
[07:40] Liam Chen: For networking: you recommended PrivateLink. Any tradeoffs?
[07:46] Priya Anand: PrivateLink reduces variability but costs more per GB. With large streaming workloads, cost matters. For p99-critical endpoints, we usually recommend PrivateLink for control; for lower-tier traffic, use public with retries and caching.
[07:59] Nora Blake: Can you recap recommended config for us?
[08:05] Ethan Miller: Sure: 1) Run the Redwood benchmark (we'll do this). 2) Keep pods warm, prefetch KV and enable persistent GPU-resident KV for critical endpoints. 3) Increase streaming chunk size slightly or hybrid strategy. 4) Adaptive batching with 40-60ms window under low QPS. 5) Evaluate int8 first, 4-bit if acceptable on your evals. 6) Consider PrivateLink or Dedicated for p99 tightening.
[08:29] Aisha Patel: Sounds good. Who's owning the benchmark?
[08:33] Ethan Miller: We'll own it (Ethan/Priya/Carlos). We'll need access and the seq histogram, which you said Marco and Samir will provide.
[08:42] Marco Ruiz: I'll send traffic replay and a sample dataset by tomorrow.
[08:46] Priya Anand: We'll also provide a config patch for your runtime and chart with p50/p95/p99.
[08:53] Liam Chen: Timeline: run the bench, then reconvene with results and a Dedicated pilot proposal?
[08:59] Ethan Miller: Yes, plan for a follow-up next Tue 2026-03-24 to review numbers and pilot pricing.
[09:05] Nora Blake: Ok thanks, appreciate the actionability.
[09:09] Carlos Vega: We'll share the deck and bench spreadsheet right after.
[09:13] (end of meeting)

Notes: Transcript contains a few mis-hearings and occasional placeholder labels; attachments referenced: solstice-bench.xlsx, redwood-dedicated-arch.pdf, redwood-soc2-pack.zip. Some technical terms may be abbreviated (KV, NLB, NAT).
